passages.t: ‘As the deer pants for streams of water’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah” (verse 1). Then comes one of the best-known pictures in the Psalms. “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God” (verse 1).

He is thirsty for God himself. “My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (verse 2). He has been crying so much that tears feel like his meals, “while men ask me all day long, ‘Where is your God?’” (verse 3).

He remembers better days. He used to walk with the crowd, “leading the procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise” (verse 4).

Then he does something unusual. He speaks to himself. “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 42 opens Book Two of the Psalms, which runs to Psalm 72 (the book page explains the five books). It also begins a group of psalms headed ‘of the sons of Korah’ (42 to 49). The book page says who they were: a family of temple singers. Korah himself rebelled against Moses, but Numbers notes, “However, the line of Korah did not die out” (Numbers 26:11). His descendants ended up serving at the very house of God this psalm longs for.

One thing changes in Book Two, and you can see it in your Bible. In Psalms 1 to 41 the Hebrew uses God's personal name, shown as ‘the LORD’, about 270 times, and the ordinary word for God, Elohim, about 50 times. In Psalms 42 to 72 it turns round: Elohim about 200 times and ‘the LORD’ fewer than 30. Scholars call Psalms 42 to 83 the Elohistic Psalms because of it. No one knows for sure why the collectors did this.

In the hills of Israel many streams flowed only in the rainy season. A deer looking for water in summer might find a dry bed. The picture is not mild longing. It is an animal that needs water to live.

Verse 4 recalls the great feasts, when Israel went up to Jerusalem in crowds (Deuteronomy 16:16). The singer once led them. Now he cannot go.
passages.later:
Other psalms use the same thirst. David wrote in the wilderness, “my soul thirsts for You” (Psalm 63:1), and another son of Korah sang, “my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God” (Psalm 84:2).

Jesus stood up at a feast in Jerusalem and called out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37).

The mocking question ‘Where is your God?’ was thrown at Jesus too. At the cross men said, “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43).
passages.hard:
Is a believer allowed to feel downcast? This psalm says yes. The singer loves God and is still low. He does not pretend. He talks honestly to God and to himself.

No one should read this psalm and decide what is wrong with someone else. It does not say why he is low, and it gives no single cure. If ‘my tears have been my food both day and night’ is true of you now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Notice the move in verse 5. He does not only listen to his feelings. He talks back to them. He asks his own soul a question, and then he tells it what to do: hope in God.

You can do that. You can say to yourself, ‘Why are you so low?’ and then answer, ‘Put your hope in God.’ It is not pretending to be fine. Verse 5 still says ‘downcast’. It is choosing where to look while you are still low.

passages.t: ‘Deep calls to deep’, and ‘Where is your God?’
passages.happening:
The second half begins lower still. “O my God, my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon” (verse 6). He is far away in the north.

Now water is not something he longs for. It is something drowning him. “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me” (verse 7).

Yet a quiet line comes in the middle. “The LORD decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (verse 8).

Then the questions return. “I say to God my Rock, ‘Why have You forgotten me?’” (verse 9). His enemies ask again, “Where is your God?” (verse 10). And he speaks to his soul again, in almost the same words as before (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Mount Hermon is the tallest mountain in the region, in the far north. Its snow and springs feed the Jordan River. The roar of water there was loud. A hearer in Jerusalem would know how far that was from the temple.

Mount Mizar is named nowhere else. Its name means ‘small mountain’. Some think it was a local peak. Others hear a contrast with Zion, the hill he cannot reach.

‘Deep’ is the Hebrew tehom, the word for the deep waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). For an Israelite the deep waters stood for chaos and danger. He calls them ‘Your’ waves. Even the flood that seems to drown him belongs to God.

Verse 8 is the one place in the psalm where God is called ‘the LORD’, his personal name.
passages.later:
Jonah, sinking in the sea, prayed almost the same words: “all Your breakers and waves swept over me” (Jonah 2:3).

On the night before he died, Jesus said in Gethsemane, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death” (Mark 14:34). Many readers hear in this an echo of the refrain of Psalms 42 and 43. It is an echo, not a quotation. But it suggests that Jesus knew the downcast soul from the inside.
passages.asks:
Verse 8 sits between two floods. Even here, he says, God's love is sent by day and his song is there at night. He does not feel it in every line. He says it anyway.

The psalm does not end with the problem solved. The refrain comes twice here, and once more in Psalm 43. Hope is not a single decision. It is a thing you say to yourself again and again. Read on into Psalm 43, which finishes the poem.
